CausalChain: Hypoxia → HIF stabilization → Upregulation of miR‐210 → Suppression of iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins (e.g. ISCU) → Downregulation of mitochondrial complex function → Reduced ROS production → Attenuated TKI-induced oxidative stress → Drug resistance. Therefore, miR‐210 inhibition would restore mitochondrial activity and ROS production, enhancing TKI efficacy.
Hypothesis: In hepatocellular carcinoma, targeted inhibition of HIF‐induced miR‐210 will restore mitochondrial respiration and elevate ROS production, thereby re-sensitizing hypoxic tumor cells to tyrosine kinase inhibitors and overcoming drug resistance.
Abstract: Recent studies indicate that hypoxia‐induced metabolic reprogramming, orchestrated largely by hypoxia‐inducible factors (HIFs), plays a central role in the drug resistance of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In hypoxic conditions, HIF‐induced transcription leads to a shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, activation of lactate and adenosinergic metabolic pathways, and diversion of metabolites into the serine synthesis pathway. One underexplored aspect in this milieu is the contribution of microRNA‐210, a robust HIF target, which downregulates components of the iron‐sulfur cluster assembly and mitochondrial function. We hypothesize that HIF‐mediated upregulation of miR‐210 dampens mitochondrial respiration and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, thereby reducing the efficacy of tyrosine kinase inhibitors that rely on ROS‐induced cytotoxicity. Inhibition of miR‐210 may restore mitochondrial electron transport and increase ROS levels in HCC cells, thus sensitizing them to standard therapies. This approach could represent a novel strategy to counteract hypoxia‐driven drug resistance in HCC.
